title: 'Something does not smell right': As lawsuits plague R.I.'s 'Conjuring' house, judge says the cases are a mess - The Boston Globe
excerpt: The Burrillville, R.I., farmhouse made famous by the horror movie franchise is now haunting courtrooms
content:

A lawsuit filed by Needham Bank brought the saga back into court last week.

Also involved in this lawsuit is Jason Hawes, the Rhode Island-based star of the SyFy television series “Ghost Hunters.” He is listed as an interested party because Nuñez signed an agreement to sell the property to Hawes in December 2025. Hawes filed a warranty deed for the house in June.

But in court on Tuesday, Darigan denied a motion filed by Hawes that sought to compel Summit & Stone to issue a payoff statement so Hawes could pay the remaining mortgage balance. The motion was denied without prejudice, meaning it could be filed again.

Darigan said she is “extremely concerned” and suggested several cases surrounding the property be assigned to a single judge who could better keep tabs on “all of the different tentacles.”

“This case and all the affiliated cases are a mess,” she said.

There are “too many open questions,” Darigan said. Hawes’s ties to the property have not been determined by a court, and it’s still unclear what Summit & Stone “is holding and what is owed,” she said.

“That [is] a fundamental issue that needs to be resolved,” Darigan said. “Is the deed from December a valid deed, and how do we go about consummating the sale completely?”

Hawes’s claims to the property have been challenged before.

Nuñez’s sister, Elizabeth Greenhalgh, of Utah, filed a lawsuit last year alleging Nuñez had been “experiencing serious mental health issues” that impaired her judgment when she signed a warranty deed and power of attorney agreement last year authorizing Julia Demay, a woman described in court documents as her friend, to sell the property to Hawes for $1.3 million. The complaint alleged Hawes was taking advantage of “Nuñez’s lack of legal capacity” for his own personal and financial gain.

Nicole M. Labonte, an attorney for Hawes, said earlier this year that a notary involved in preparing the documents in October 2025 later indicated she had not notarized the documents properly. Nuñez then signed a deed in December with a different notary, Labonte said.

Greenhalgh’s lawsuit was dismissed in April, after a judge found she did not have legal standing. In an affidavit filed in August, Greenhalgh wrote Nuñez has maintained she did not sell the house to Hawes.

Greenhalgh had also petitioned the Suffolk County Probate and Family Court in Massachusetts to appoint her as Nuñez’s guardian and conservator so she could manage her sister’s affairs. On Tuesday, however, a stipulation was filed indicating Greenhalgh and other parties involved — including Nuñez and Demay — had agreed to drop the matter.

“It wasn’t sustainable,” Isaac H. Peres, an attorney representing Demay, said Thursday.

Peres said a medical evaluation for Nuñez was not completed, and a required medical certificate was never filed.

“In the future, if they ever got a certificate, they can come back,” Peres said.

Court filings state Nuñez, who was listed as living in Dorchester, now resides in Utah. Attorneys for Nuñez and Greenhalgh did not return requests for comment.

Summit & Stone also accused Hawes of fraud and exploitation. Labonte, in court in Rhode Island on Tuesday, called those claims “defamatory.”

Summit & Stone filed a petition in January asking a court to place Bale Fire into receivership, a process similar to bankruptcy in state court, citing an outstanding balance on the mortgage of approximately $1.2 million. A judge denied the motion in February.

On Tuesday, Vincent A. Indeglia, an attorney for Summit & Stone, said the company bought the house with the thought that “it was either going to get cash or it was going to get the property, one or the other.”

Darigan said she is “very skeptical about Summit & Stone’s motivations.”

“I don’t buy the arguments that they are concerned about liability to Bale Fire, or to Nuñez, or to anybody else,” Darigan said. “... In a contested property situation, [it] seems to me that people would sit down, particularly a lender, would sit down and have a conversation …. That’s not happening.”

“Fundamental questions about who has what rights and what interests” need to be answered, Darigan concluded at the end of Tuesday’s hour-long hearing.

“Once that’s decided, I think some things can fall into place,” she said. “This case is a problem.”

Material from previous Globe stories was used in this report.
